sec.title: Background
sec.p: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is susceptible to abiotic factors during its growth period, such as salt and drought. The germination stage is the initial growth stage of wheat growth, when wheat is particularly sensitive to salt and drought stress.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In this study, the genetic basis of salt and drought tolerance in wheat was explored using a recombinant inbred lines (RILs) population consisting of 188 lines derived from a cross between the cultivars Kenong9204 (KN9204) and Jing411 (J411). The KJ-RIL lines and their parents were evaluated under 100 mM NaCl salt stress and 10% polyethylene glycol 6000 (PEG-6000) induced drought stress. A principal component analysis (PCA) showed that the cumulative contribution rate of the four principal components was 87.16% and 85.62% under salt and drought stress, respectively. A total of 16 salt-tolerant and five drought-tolerant lines were selected using the membership function and 52 putative additive quantitative trait loci (QTLs) and 251 epistatic QTLs (eQTLs) for eight traits were detected in the KJ-RILs. Among the 251 eQTLs, 19, 32, 67, 21, 27, 29, 32, and 24 pairwise eQTLs were observed for sheath length, seedling length, maximum root length, root number, seedling fresh weight, root fresh weight, seedling dry weight, and root dry weight, respectively. The 52 putative additive QTLs were found in all of the 21 wheat chromosomes except 1A, 2D, and 4A. The QTLs accounted for 3.92–13.26% of the phenotypic variation with logarithm of the odds values ranging from 2.52–6.91. A total of seven stable QTLs were detected: qShl-1D, qShl-3B, qSl-4D, qMrl-1D, qRn-2A.3, qRn-4B, and qRdw-7D, and three major QTLs were detected: qShl-4B, qRn-3B, and qRfw-7D. Among them, qShl-3B was a stable major QTL that explained 10.96%–12.02% of the variation rate and the most favorable allele came from KN9204. In addition, an InDel marker closely linked to qShl-3B was developed and validated in 188 RILs.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Different putative additive QTLs and epistatic QTLs (eQTLs) located on most of the 21 wheat chromosomes were detected for the studied traits. Of which, a total of seven stable QTLs and three major QTLs were detected. In addition, an InDel marker closely linked to the stable major QTL, qShl-3B was developed and validated in 188 RILs, providing important information for the genetic improvement and development of salt and drought tolerance wheat varieties.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is a globally important food crop; its total area and output are third only to rice and maize; and it provides about 20% of human energy [1]. It is an important cereal crop that makes a significant contribution to food and nutritional security across the globe. However, wheat production and productivity are affected by several abiotic stresses, such as drought, heat, cold, and salt stress [2].

It has been estimated that the global salt-affected land area is more than 800 million ha (6% of the total global land area) and it has been continuously increasing year by year due to climate change and land clearance [1, 3]. Soil salinity severely damages plant growth by lowering the growth rate, reducing the number of tillers, accelerating the senescence of old leaves, decreasing photosynthetic capability, and altering reproductive development. These effects lead to significant reductions in the final agricultural yield [4, 5]. The impact of saline stress on crop yield can be reduced by cultivating saline tolerant crop varieties that effectively resist the adverse effects of soil salinization. Salt tolerance in wheat is a quantitative trait controlled by multiple genes and the mechanism associated with salt tolerance is complex. Exploring new genetic loci for salt tolerance in wheat and its related species and applying them to breeding programs has become the most economical, effective, and safe method to cultivate salt tolerant wheat varieties [6]. Ma et al. [7] used Opata85 × W7987 hybridization under salt stress to conduct a linkage analysis of 114 families and identified 47 QTLs for root fresh weigh (RFW), root dry weight (RDW), root fresh weight index, shoot fresh weight index, and other traits at the germination and seedling stages; Xu et al. [8] used 182 recombinant inbred lines to locate salt tolerance QTLs at the seedling stage. A total of 29 additive QTLs and 17 epistatic QTLs (eQTLs) were detected for maximum root length (MRL), shoot height, RDW, etc.; and Luo et al. [9] used an F7 recombinant inbred line (RIL) population to locate salt tolerance QTLs for sheath length (SHL), plant height, and number of grains per spike, etc. at two levels of salt stress.

The increasing global population and the increase in extreme weather events are significant threats to global food security and sustainability. Among the many environmental challenges, water shortage is a major constraint that affects all aspects of plant growth and development and agricultural productivity [10, 11]. Drought is a major stress factor that limits crop yields [12] and selective breeders face serious challenges when attempting to ensure food security through the production of new varieties [13, 14]. Water scarcity can affect wheat at all developmental stages, such as germination, early seedling growth, flowering, and grain filling, and ultimately leads to reduced yields and quality [15]. Insufficient water during early seedling growth slows root and shoot development and makes plants more susceptible to pests and diseases [10, 16]. Previous studies have reported on drought tolerance at the wheat germination stage using QTL mapping [17–20]. Ren et al. [21] detected 18 drought tolerance related QTLs based on their DD-value and they explained 2.7%–6.5% of the phenotypic variation. Liu et al. [20] detected 28 drought-tolerant loci for coleoptile length, seedling height, longest root length, root number, and another 12 phenotypic traits at the germination stage. They were all located on 12 chromosomes and explained 5.61%–64.22% of the phenotypic variation. Khanna et al. [22] detected seven stable wheat QTLs for flag leaf area, flag leaf length, and flag leaf width under drought stress.

In this study, drought and salt stress were simulated to identify related traits at the germination stage. The objectives of this study were to (1) screen-out salt and drought resistant materials from lines produced via a cross between Kenong9204 (KN9204) and Jing411 (J411) (KJ-RILs) based on their comprehensive evaluation value; (2) determine the putative additive QTLs and epistatic QTLs in the KJ-RIL lines under salt and drought stress; and (3) develop relevant molecular markers for molecular-assisted breeding.

sec.title: Plant materials
sec.p: The common wheat variety KN9204 was released in 2002 and J411 is an elite parent in the northern winter wheat region. Compared to J411, KN9204 is a semi-dwarfing cultivar with a wider flag leaf, smaller seed size, and a larger percentage of ear-bearing tillers. A total of 188 lines (F8:9) from RILs derived from a cross between KN9204 and J411 were used.

sec.title: Hydroponic culture and experimental design
sec.p: This study designed preliminary experimental concentration gradients of 5%, 10%, and 15% for PEG-6000, along with 50, 100, and 150 mM for NaCl. The results demonstrated that 10% PEG-6000 and 100 mM NaCl were the optimal concentrations for the KJ-RIL population research. In this study, pure water was used as a control check (CK), and a 100 mM NaCl was prepared by dissolving 5.84 g of NaCl in purified water, followed by dilution to a final volume of 1 L. Similarly, a 10% PEG-6000 solution was prepared by dissolving 100 g of PEG-6000 in purified water and bringing the volume to 1 L.

The experiment was performed in a greenhouse. The salt and drought stress responses of the 188 kJ-RILs and their parents were evaluated in a hydroponic culture containing purified water (CK), salt stress (S, 100 mM NaCl) and drought stress (D, 10% PEG-6000) inducing compounds. The experiments were conducted in randomized complete blocks (RCBD) with three replications.

A total of 30 plump seeds of each line were surface-sterilized in 5% NaClO for 5 min, rinsed with water, and then germinated in hydroponic plastic boxes (32 cm × 24 cm) for 7 days. The greenhouse had a 20 h/4 h light/dark cycle and the temperature was maintained at 22 °C during the growth period (Supplementary Fig. 1). In this hydroponic experiment, seeds were evenly arranged, and the solution was fill up before covering the hydroponic plastic box lid. The box lid was opened on the fifth day, and phenotypic measurements were conducted on the eighth day. No additional solution was required throughout the entire experimental process. On the 8 th day, 10 uniform seedlings from each line were selected and eight different traits were assessed: SHL, seedling length (SL), MRL, root number (RN), seedling fresh weight (SFW), RFW, seedling dry weight (SDW), and RDW. The average SHL of 10 uniform seedlings was recorded to the nearest cm by measuring from the base of the seedling to the coleoptile tip. The longest seedling root was used to measure RL. The RFW was measured after removing any excess water by pressing the roots gently with tissue paper. The RDW and SDW were measured after drying samples to a constant weight in an oven at 70℃ for 24 h.

sec.title: Data analysis
sec.p: The maximum, minimum, mean, range of variation, standard deviation, and coefficient of variation (CV) of the data were obtained using SPSS 21.0 (SPSS Statistics 21.0, IBM Corp. Armonk, NY, USA). Broad-sense heritability (H2) and BLUE datasets for all traits under control (CK), S, and D conditions were analyzed using QGA Statistics software (QGA Statistics1.0, Zhejiang University, 2004) and the detailed steps can be found in Cai et al. [23]. Correlation analysis was performed and visualized using the “corrplot” package in R software.

sec.title: Calculation of the salt tolerance coefficient, drought tolerance coefficient, and comprehensive evaluation value
sec.p: The stress tolerance index, principal component analysis, and membership function calculation were carried out according to previous studies [24–26].

where SC is the salt-tolerance coefficient, DC is the drought-tolerance coefficient, and XS, XD, and XCK are the trait values under salt stress (S), drought stress (D), and CK conditions, respectively.

U ZSj is the membership function value for salt tolerance based on the particular phenotype trait, ZSj is the jth composite indicator, and ZSmax and ZSmin are the maximum and minimum values of the jth SC, respectively. U ZDj is the membership function value for drought tolerance based on the particular phenotype trait, ZDj is the jth composite indicator, and ZDmax and ZDmin are the maximum and minimum values of the jth DC, respectively. Wj is the weight of the jth comprehensive index and Pj is the variance contribution rate of the jth comprehensive index. The membership function value (U) of the comprehensive index for each wheat variety was calculated using Eqs. (3) and (4). The contribution rate for each comprehensive index was used to calculate the weight of the principal components and the index weight and membership function value were used to calculate the comprehensive evaluation value for salt or drought resistance (DD or DS value, respectively). The D value is the comprehensive evaluation value for the salt resistance or drought resistance shown by a particular phenotype, as determined by a comprehensive evaluation of various wheat cultivars under S or D. A cluster analysis was carried out using SPSS 21.0 software.

Highly salt-tolerant lines were defined as 0.8 < DS < 1.0, the salt-tolerant lines were defined as 0.6 < DS < 0.8, the moderately salt-tolerant lines were defined as 0.4 < DS < 0.6, the salt-sensitive lines were defined as 0.2 < DS < 0.4, and the salt weak sensitive lines were defined as 0.0 < DS < 0.2.

sec.title: QTL analysis
sec.p: A high-density genetic linkage map of the KJ-RILs was constructed using a Wheat 660K SNP array [27] and IciMapping 4.2 software was used to create the genetic linkage map and perform the QTL analysis. The pre-adjusted mapping parameters for IciMapping 4.2 were set at method = inclusive composite interval mapping (ICIM), step = 1.0 cM, PIN = 0.001, and a logarithm of the odds (LOD) ≥ 2.5. The QTLs that had more than 10% of their phenotypic variation explained (PVE) and LOD values > 3.0 were considered to be major QTLs and QTLs detected in two datasets were considered to be stable QTLs.

The interaction effects among the eQTLs were also analyzed. In the analysis, the ICIM-EPI in the BIP module found in IciMapping 4.2 was used to perform the mapping analysis and a 5 Mb walking speed was chosen for all the pairwise QTLs. The P value inclusion threshold was 0.0001, and the LOD threshold was 3.0.

sec.title: InDel markers design
sec.p: Based on 10 × genome resequencing of KN9204 and J411, a 60 bp insertion and deletion (InDel) polymorphic DNA sequence was identified at position KN3B:195572704 of the KN9204 genome, which was subsequently utilized for developing polymorphic molecular markers. Using the PrimerServer in WheatOmics1.0 (http://202.194.139.32/PrimerServer/), polymorphic InDel PCR primers were designed with the forward primer sequence 5′-CCAGCACGTCAAGACCCAA-3′ and the reverse primer sequence 5′-CTCCTGGGTCACTTGAGGC-3′.

sec.title: Phenotypic evaluation of the RILs
sec.p: The phenotypic characteristics (eight traits) of the 188 kJ-RILs and their parents were investigated under CK, S, and D conditions (Table 1). According to the results of ANOVA, under CK, KN9204 had greater RDW and lower SFW and RFW than J411, but there were no significant differences among the other traits. Under S stress, KN9204 had longer SL and heavier RFW than J411, whereas the MRL for J411 were longer than those for KN9204. Under D stress, KN9204 had longer SHL and MRL and heavier RFW than J411.

sec.p: The maximum, minimum, and mean values of most traits under S and D stress were lower than those of the CK. This indicates that wheat growth was inhibited under both stresses. SHL and RN were less affected by stress. The phenotypic variation among the measured traits varied considerably among the 188 kJ-RILs. The CV under CK, S, and D ranged from 7.50%−29.31%, 3.23%−26.49%, and 7.18%−25.53%, respectively. The CV for RFW under CK was the largest at 29.31%, indicating that the phenotypic variation associated with RFW was high. The H2 for all measured traits was 15.58%–44.41% and the absolute values for trait skewness and kurtosis were less than 1.0 in most cases, which showed that the phenotype values followed a normal distribution and that the traits were controlled by multiple QTLs.

sec.title: Correlation analysis of the eight traits
sec.p: There were significant correlations among the eight traits (Fig. 1). Under CK, most traits were highly significantly and positively correlated, among which SDW and RDW had the highest correlation coefficient at 0.68 (P ≤ 0.001). There was a negative correlation between SHL and RN (−0.17, P ≤ 0.05).

There was a highly significant positive association between SL and SFW under both S and D stresses, with correlation coefficients of 0.54 and 0.56, respectively (P ≤ 0.001); very highly significant positive correlations between SFW and RFW under both S and D (0.70 and 0.73, respectively, P ≤ 0.001); and highly significant positive correlations between SDW and RDW under both stresses. SFW and RFW were positively correlated with RDW under S stress, but there was a significantly negative correlation between SHL and RN (−0.15, P ≤ 0.05). SDW and RDW had the highest correlation coefficient at 0.73 (P ≤ 0.001). Under D stress, all traits except for SHL had highly significant positive correlations with RDW and all the traits had highly significant positive correlations with SL.

sec.title: Principle component analysis of the eight traits under salt and drought stress
sec.p: A PCA of the eight tested traits extracted six principal components under S and D conditions (Table 2). Under S, the variance contribution rates for the CI comprehensive indices (CI1 to CI6) were 25.13%, 19.42%, 13.51%, 11.01%, 9.96%, and 8.13%, respectively, with a cumulative contribution rate of 87.16%. Under D, the variance contribution rates for CI1 to CI6 were 24.77%, 15.84%, 12.92%, 12.60%, 10.50%, and 8.99%, respectively, with a cumulative contribution rate of 85.62%. The first factors contributed more than 20% under both stresses. The original eight single traits could be converted into six new independent comprehensive indices, which covered most of the information regarding wheat stress tolerance. The PCA fully reflected the primary and secondary functions of the wheat indicators screened for salt and drought tolerance and could be used to comprehensively evaluate the drought tolerance differences between the different wheat cultivars.

sec.title: Comprehensive evaluation of the KJ-RILs and their parents
sec.p: Comprehensive values for salt and drought tolerance (DS and DD values, respectively) were calculated and the salt and drought tolerances of the wheat cultivars were ranked according to the D value (Table S1, Table S2). Under S, the DS value for KJ15 was highest, reaching 0.781, followed by KJ11, KJ12, and KJ14. The DS value for KJ106 was the lowest (0.297) indicating that it was less tolerant to S. Under D conditions, KJ11 had the highest DD value (0.630), followed by KJ33, KJ19, and KJ34. The DD value for KJ106 was lowest (0.202), indicating that it was less tolerant to D.

A cluster analysis was performed on the 188 kJ-RILs and their parents under S and D conditions and they were clustered into five categories (Table 3). There were 16 salt-tolerant lines (KJ7, KJ8, KJ11, KJ12, KJ14, KJ15, KJ51, KJ53, KJ54, KJ110, KJ111, KJ118, KJ131, KJ155, KJ156, and KJ169), 157 moderately salt-tolerant lines (KJ1, KJ2, KJ3, and KJ4, etc.), and 17 salt-sensitive lines (KJ37, KJ38, KJ46, KJ48, KJ62, KJ65, KJ83, KJ87, KJ89, KJ97, KJ98, KJ106, KJ120, KJ122, KJ123, KJ124, and KJ148). There were five drought-tolerant lines (KJ11, KJ12, KJ19, KJ33, and KJ34), 153 moderately drought-tolerant lines (KJ1, KJ2, and KJ3, etc.), and 32 drought-sensitive lines (KJ10, KJ25, KJ67, KJ69, and KJ75, etc.). Therefore, KJ12 was a salt and drought tolerant line. In addition, KN9204 and J411 were classified as moderately tolerant lines under both S and D conditions.

sec.title: Epistatic QTL mapping of the eight traits
sec.p: A total of 251 eQTLs for the eight traits were identified in the datasets (C-BLUE, S-BLUE, and D-BLUE) among which, 19, 32, 67, 21, 27, 29, 32, and 24 pairwise eQTLs were observed for SHL, SL, MRL, RN, SFW, RFW, SDW, and RDW, respectively (Table S3; Fig. 2).

caption.p: Chromosomal distribution of additive-by-additive epistatic interactions among the eight traits identified by IciMapping 4.2 in the three datasets (C-BLUE, S-BLUE, and D-BLUE). SHL: sheath length, SL: seedling length, MRL: maximum root length, RN: root number, SFW: seedling fresh weight, RFW: root fresh weight, SDW: seedling dry weight, and RDW: root dry weight

sec.p: A total of 19 significant interactions were identified for SHL, which together accounted for 42.63% of the total SHL phenotypic variation (Table S3; Fig. 2). One pairwise eQTL (3B: 57.17 Mb and 7D: 632.79 Mb) accounted for 4.03% of the SHL phenotypic variation and nine of the 19 pairwise eQTLs had negative additive-by-additive interaction effects, indicating that the epistatic effects of the recombinant lines between the pairwise loci decreased SHL.

A total of 32 pairwise eQTLs for SL were found in the three datasets and together they accounted for 67.05% of the total SL phenotypic variation. Fourteen of the 32 significant eQTL interaction effects were positive, suggesting that SL decreased after most of the recombination events between the corresponding pairwise points. One eQTL (2D: 491.75 Mb) had significant interactive effects with four random eQTLs, i.e., 3A: 325.76 Mb, 4A: 506.91 Mb, 5B: 445.32 Mb, and 6D: 240.44 Mb, which accounted for 4.15%, 4.15%, 4.15%, and 4.17% of the phenotypic variance, respectively. Another eQTL (7D: 567.79 Mb) had significant interactive effects with two random eQTLs, i.e., 1A: 100.13 Mb and 1D: 5.13 Mb, accounting for 1.79% and 1.15% of the phenotypic variance, respectively.

A total of 67 significant interactions were identified for MRL, which together accounted for 109.73% of the total MRL phenotypic variation. Two pairwise eQTLs (3A: 345.76 Mb and 3A: 410.76 Mb and 2D: 636.75 Mb and 5B: 285.32 Mb) accounted for 4.39% and 4.02% of the MRL phenotypic variation, respectively. A total of 11 eQTLs were able to interact with more than one locus.

A total of 21 pairwise eQTLs were found for RN in the three datasets and together they accounted for 46.37% of the total RN phenotypic variation. One pairwise eQTL (5B: 255.32 Mb and 5B: 260.32 Mb) accounted for 7.10% of the RN phenotypic variation and 11 of the 21 significant eQTL interaction effects were positive and suggested that RN decreased after most of the recombination events between the corresponding pairwise points.

A total of 27 significant interactions were identified for SFW, which together accounted for 53.98% of the total SFW phenotypic variation. Three pairwise eQTLs (2D: 211.75 Mb and 6D: 395.44 Mb, 3A: 405.76 Mb and 3B: 742.17 Mb, and 3A: 410.76 Mb and 5B: 540.32 Mb) accounted for 4.31%, 4.82%, and 4.78% of the SFW phenotypic variation. One eQTL (3B: 742.17 Mb) had significant interactive effects on two random eQTLs, i.e., 3A: 405.76 Mb and 7B: 715.06 Mb, accounting for 4.82% and 1.81% of the phenotypic variance, respectively. Another eQTL (5B: 560.32 Mb) also had significant interactive effects on two random eQTLs, (1B: 535.16 Mb and 3B: 327.16 Mb), accounting for 1.50% and 1.31% of the phenotypic variance, respectively.

A total of 29 pairwise eQTLs were found for RFW in the three datasets and together they accounted for 56.92% of the total RFW phenotypic variation. Three pairwise eQTLs (4A: 316.91 Mb and 4B: 25.70 Mb, 2B: 50.06 Mb and 5B: 230.32 Mb, and 3A: 390.76 Mb and 3A: 695.76 Mb) accounted for 4.74%, 4.50%, and 4.57% of the RFW phenotypic variation, respectively, and nine of the 21 significant eQTL interaction effects were positive and suggested that RFW decreased after most of the recombination events between the corresponding pairwise points.

A total of 32 pairwise eQTLs were found for SDW in the three datasets and together they accounted for 64.98% of the total SDW phenotypic variation. However, the significant interactions only had minor effects and explained ≤ 4.00% of the phenotypic variation. One eQTL (2B: 135.05 Mb) had significant interactive effects with four random eQTLs, i.e., 3A: 280.76 Mb, 4A: 346.91 Mb, 5B: 200.32 Mb, and 6D: 210.44 Mb, accounting for 2.98%, 3.38%, 3.51%, and 3.61% of the phenotypic variance, respectively.

There were 24 SDW eQTLs that had significant interaction effects. The lowest phenotypic variability was 0.89% and the highest value was 4.90%. Of these, two eQTLs were able to interact with more than one locus. Eleven of the 24 significant eQTL interaction effects were positive and suggested that SDW decreased after most of the recombination events between the corresponding pairwise points.

sec.title: Additive QTL analysis
sec.p: A total of 52 putative additive QTLs for the eight traits were detected in the KJ-RILs. They were distributed across all 21 wheat chromosomes with the exception of 1A, 2D, and 4A (Table 4). Among the 52 QTLs, the additive effects of 27 QTLs were derived from the KN9204 alleles, whereas the additive effects of the other 25 QTLs were from the J411 alleles. These QTLs accounted for 3.92–13.26% of the phenotypic variation, with LOD values ranging from 2.52 to 6.91.

sec.p: A total of nine putative additive QTLs for SHL were identified in the three treatments and in the DI dataset. These QTLs individually explained 3.92–13.10% of the phenotypic variance with LOD values ranging from 2.52–6.91. KN9204 and J411 contributed three and six favorable alleles that increased SHL, respectively. and two of the nine QTLs were stable major QTLs with LOD values > 3.0 and PVE values > 10.0%. Of these, qShl-3B was a stable, major QTL that was detected under D and in the DI dataset. The LOD values were 4.18–4.20, the PVE values were 10.96–12.02%, and KN9204 contributed the positive alleles that increased SHL. QShl-4B was a major QTL, but it was only detected in the C dataset, with a PVE of 13.10%. QShl-1D (1D: 463.13 Mb–465.13 Mb) was detected under S and D conditions, but not under the CK condition. QShl-2A.1, qShl-2A.2, qShl-2B, qShl-5D, qShl-6B, and qShl-7B were treatment-dependent QTLs that were only detected in one treatment.

A total of eight putative additive QTLs for SL were identified in the three treatments and in the DI dataset. These QTLs individually explained 4.62–9.78% of the phenotypic variance with LOD values ranging from 2.56–4.22. KN9204 and J411 contributed five and three favorable alleles that increased SL, respectively. Of these, qSl-4D was a stable QTL that was detected under D and in the DI dataset and explained 6.40–6.96% of the phenotypic variation with LOD values of 2.82–3.66. J411 also contributed positive alleles that increased SL. The rest of the QTLs were all treatment-dependent and were detected under either CK, D, or S.

A total of five putative additive QTLs for MRL were identified under the two stress treatments and in the SI and DI datasets. KN9204 and J411 contributed two and three favorable alleles that increased MRL, respectively. These QTLs individually explained 6.13–7.41% of the phenotypic variance with LOD values ranging from 2.61–3.16. QMrl-1D was a stable QTL for MRL with LOD values of 2.88–3.06 and PVE values of 6.13–6.76%; qMrl-1D (D: 463.13 Mb–479.13 Mb) was detected under S and was in the SI datasets; and J411 also contributed positive alleles that increased MRL.

A total of nine putative additive QTLs for RN were identified under the three treatments and in the SI and DI datasets. These QTLs individually explained 4.57–10.12% of the phenotypic variance with LOD values ranging from 2.57–6.28. QRn-2A.3 was a stable QTL for RN with LOD values of 2.57–3.24 and PVE values of 6.71–8.09%. It was detected under S and in the SI and DI datasets. In contrast, qRn-4B (4B: 27.70 Mb–28.70 Mb) was detected after the D and CK treatments with LOD values ranging from 3.31–3.78 and PVE values of 5.43–6.73%. There was also a major QTL, qRn-3B, that explained 10.12% of the phenotypic variation with an LOD value of 6.28.

A total of five putative additive QTLs for SFW were identified under the three treatments. These QTLs individually explained 5.28–8.45% of the phenotypic variance with LOD values ranging from 2.55–3.83. All the QTLs were environment-dependent and were only detected in one treatment. KN9204 and J411 contributed three and two favorable alleles that increased SFW, respectively.

A total of three putative additive QTLs for RFW were identified under the two stress treatments and in the SI dataset. These QTLs individually explained 6.39–13.26% of the phenotypic variation with LOD values ranging from 2.57–4.32. One of the three QTLs was a major QTL with LOD values > 3.0 and PVE values > 10.0%. All three QTLs were treatment-dependent and were only detected in one treatment. KN9204 and J411 contributed two and one favorable alleles that increased RFW, respectively.

A total of seven putative additive QTLs for SDW were identified under the three treatments and in the SI dataset. These QTLs individually explained 5.79–9.88% of the phenotypic variation with LOD values ranging from 2.58–3.67. All the QTLs were treatment-dependent and were only detected in one treatment. KN9204 and J411 contributed two and five favorable alleles that increased SDW, respectively.

A total of six putative additive QTLs for RDW were identified in the two stress treatments and in the SI dataset. These QTLs individually explained 3.98–9.97% of the phenotypic variation with LOD values ranging from 2.69–6.46. KN9204 and J411 contributed three and three favorable alleles that increased RDW, respectively. QRdw-7D (7D: 19.79 Mb–20.79 Mb) was a stable QTL for RDW with LOD values of 2.81–2.97 and PVE values of 5.33–7.43% and was only detected under S and in the SI dataset. J411 also contributed positive alleles that increased RDW. QRdw-1D, qRdw-3B.1, qRdw-3B.2, qRdw-5D, and qRdw-6D were treatment-dependent QTLs that were only detected in one treatment.

sec.title: Co-localized QTLs
sec.p: A QTL for SHL (qShl-1D) that was stable under S and D was co-localized with qMrl-1D (1D: 463.13 Mb–479.13 Mb), they came from KN9204, and increased SHL and MRL (Table S4). A QTL for RFW (qRfw-2A) in the SI dataset was co-localized with qSfw-2A under S, they increased RFW and SFW and came from KN9204. A QTL for RN (qRn-2A.2) under CK was co-localized with qRn-2A.3 under S and was in the SI and DI datasets. These alleles were from J411 and KN9204, respectively, and this QTL for RN was seriously affected by the stress conditions. A QTL for SHL (qShl-2B) under D was co-localized with qRn-2B under CK. They came from KN9204 and increased RN. However, they decreased SHL. A QTL for SDW (qSdw-4B) in the SI dataset was co-localized with qShl-4B under CK, they decreased SDW and SHL, and came from KN9204. A QTL for SL (qSl-4B) under S was co-localized with qMrl-4B under D, they increased SL and MRL, and came from KN9204. A QTL for SDW (qSdw-5A) was co-localized with qRn-5A under S stress, they came from KN9204, and they increased RN, However, they decreased SDW. A QTL for RDW (qRdw-6D) under CK was co-localized with qSdw-6D in the SI dataset, they came from KN9204, and increased RDW. However, they decreased SDW.

sec.title: PCR (InDel) markers
sec.p: Based on the genome DNA sequences information of KN9204 and J411, an InDel marker was developed near the qShl-3B LOD peak at position KN:3B195572704. This marker consistently amplified distinct target fragments of 475 bp and 415 bp in KN9204 and J411, respectively, and the PCR amplification product from this marker had a clear band pattern and stable amplification and can potentially be used for the molecular breeding of wheat SHL traits (Supplementary Fig. 2). The genotypes and SHLs of the 188 kJ-RILs were analyzed in the three drought stress replicates (Supplementary Fig. 3) and the results showed that KN9204 alleles contribute to longer SHLs.

sec.title: Effect of drought and salt stress on the different traits
sec.p: The seed germination stage is the starting point of plant life and the most critical period for crops. Wheat germination rate, seedling growth, and physiological processes at the germination stage all affect the later growth conditions of the plants. There have been a number of studies on seed tolerance to S and D conditions during germination [28–33].

Drought and salt stress affect different traits to varying degrees. Sun et al. [29] found that simulated D conditions caused by 19.6% PEG-6000 inhibited the growth of the tested materials to varying degrees, among which the germination rate and dry matter weight were the most inhibited; Dhanda et al. [33] found that the seed vigor index and SL were the most sensitive to D followed by RL and SHL; and Liu et al. [20] reported that D had the greatest impact on MRL. The results from this study showed that MRL was sensitive to D and the mean values were 13.48 cm under CK and 11.02 cm under D, which was 18.2% lower than that under CK. These results were consistent with Dhanda et al. [33] and Liu et al. [30].

Peng et al. [34] found that salt stress had a significant effect on wheat SL, MRL, SFW, and RFW and that RN increased at the seedling stage and Wang et al. [35] found that salt stress had a greater impact on MRL, but a lower impact on SHL. In this study, S had the most significant effects on wheat SL, MRL, SFW, and RFW, but had little effect on SHL, RN, and RDW. These findings were consistent with those of Wang et al. [35] and Peng et al. [34]. However, a key difference was that in this study, the RN was the least affected by S, whereas Peng et al. [34] reported that the variation in RN was significant. The differences may be due to variations in experimental materials and conditions.

sec.title: QTL clusters detected in the KJ-RILs
sec.p: It is useful to identify the co-localized QTLs conferring multiple traits and the yield-related traits were previously QTL mapped using the same genetic population [23, 36–40]. Several QTL regions identified in this study were mapped to the same or adjacent chromosomal regions for yield-related traits highlighted in the previous studies. Qin et al. [36] located QTLs for the plant height component index and the third internode component index in the 25.70 Mb–66.1 Mb range on chromosome 4B (Table S5) and Meng et al. [37] and Fan et al. [38] found QTLs for thousand-kernel weight, kernel weight, and flag leaf width in this region. In this study, qSdw-4B, qRn-4B, and qShl-4B were located between 4B: 22.70 Mb–35.70 Mb, which was the same region reported in previous reports. The plant height gene Rht-B1 (4B: 30.860 Mb–30.8630 Mb) was also found in this region; therefore, this locus may contain multiple important genes. Yu et al. [39] located QTLs related to the fourth internode diameter and the fifth internode diameter in another region of chromosome 4B (4B: 628.70 Mb–668.70 Mb) and Cai et al. [23] also identified a QTL related to spike number per plant in this region. In this study, qSl-4B and qMrl-4B under S and D were detected in the same region of 4B. This suggested that this region should be investigated further in future studies.

The QTL qEbtr-KJ-5B.1 [23] has been detected in the range 5B: 576.32 Mb–607.22 Mb and was co-located with the flag leaf width QTL qFlw-5B [40]. The QTL qSdw-5B (5B: 581.32 Mb) was also detected in the same region in this study. The QTLs for spike number per plant (qSnpp-KJ-6B), flag leaf width (qFlw-6B), and plant height (qPh-6B) have been shown to be co-located in the 6B: 438.76 Mb–506.76 Mb region [23, 38, 41]. In this study, qRfw-6B and qSfw-6B were detected in the 6B: 437.76 Mb–665.74 Mb region, but they were only detected under D. This suggested that there may be a drought tolerance gene at this region and that it might affect spike number per plant and thus wheat yield, Therefore, this region should be investigated in future studies. Another QTL cluster was 7B: 637.06 Mb–683.06 Mb. Qin et al. [36] located the first internode component index qFiitci-KJ-7B.1 and Yu et al. [39] located the third internode diameter qID-3-kJ-7B in this region. The results from this study showed that qSdw-7B and qShl-7B were also located in this region. Future studies should use fine mapping to investigate whether these QTL clusters are major QTLs with multiple effects or linked QTLs that affect multiple traits.

sec.title: Comparison of the QTLs detected in this study with those identified in previous reports
sec.p: Knowledge about salt tolerance loci and genes is required if the breeding of salt-tolerant varieties by marker-assisted selection is to be accelerated. Previous studies have investigated many traits under different levels of salt stress at the seedling stage and adult stage using QTL mapping and genome wide association studies (GWAS) [2, 42, 43]. A genome-wide linkage analysis was performed on the root traits and the relative root coefficients of the wheat recombinant inbred population (310 lines) using the cross Berkut × Worrakatta under normal and salt stress and 10 QTLs related to root traits were obtained. Two QTLs related to the salt tolerance shown by roots were obtained for wheat and they were distributed on chromosomes 2A (2A: 10.59 Mb–13.32 Mb) (the position in this paragraph is corresponding to CS1.0) and 3B (3B: 813.50 Mb–822.93 Mb) [44]. In this study, qRfw-2A in the SI dataset and qSfw-2A under S were also found near the same location in 2A (2A: 39.93 Mb–56.93 Mb) and qSl-3B under CK was detected near the same position in chromosome 3B (3B: 795.17 Mb). Devi et al. [2] detected three QTLs for Na+ content on chromosomes 5D (5D: 310.28 Mb–496.32 Mb), 6A (6A: 549.52 Mb–595.38 Mb), and 7D (7D: 13.46 Mb–58.26 Mb) under S. In this study, the QTLs for RDW, RFW, and SFW were found on chromosomes 5D (5D: 457.62 Mb), 6A (6A: 611.01 Mb), and 7D (7D: 13.79 Mb–20.79 Mb) under S. Masoudi et al. [31] also identified a QTL associated with the root K+/Na+ concentration ratio under S on chromosome 7D (5.8 Mb–41.4 Mb). The results from this study overlapped with those of previous studies. A QTL related to seedling length under S has been reported at 22.26 Mb–36.01 Mb on chromosome 4B, whereas in this study, a QTL for seedling length under S was found at about 640.70 Mb on chromosome 4B, which was a different locus from that of Luo et al. [45].

A number of studies on wheat involving QTL interval mapping and GWAS have already been conducted. As a result, a large number of QTLs have been reported for several traits related to drought tolerance. These traits include SHL, water-soluble carbohydrates, root system, grain yield, and other related traits recorded under D [46, 47]. Khalid et al. [48] identified QTLs associated with SDW under D on chromosome 3D (3D: 363.87 Mb–554.16 Mb) and a QTL for SL was detected on chromosome 4D (4D: 566.80 Mb). Nagy et al. [49] identified QTLs associated with RDW under D at the 18.67 Mb–18.87 Mb position on chromosome 3B. In this study, qRdw-3B.1 was detected on chromosome 3B (3B: 35.17 Mb) under CK, qSdw-3D was detected on chromosome 3D at 464.08 Mb in the SI dataset, and qSl-4D was detected on chromosome 4D at 506.53 Mb–508.53 Mb under D. Yu et al. [39] identified a QTL associated with RFW under D at 705.85 Mb on chromosome 5B and in this study, a QTL for MRL was also detected at 685.32 Mb on chromosome 5B in the DI dataset, which meant that there may be a drought-related gene in this region. Ahmed et al. [50] found a QTL related to SL under D at the 185.12 Mb position on chromosome 6B and in this study, a QTL associated with SL was detected on chromosome 6B at 675.76 Mb under D, which was different from the physical locations reported in previous studies.

QShl-3B was a stable and major QTL under D and the locus was not found in previous studies, which meant that it was a new QTL. This may be an important QTL for drought tolerance and should be investigated.

sec.title: S-specific QTLs and D-specific QTLs
sec.p: In this study, of the 52 detected QTLs, 71.15% (17 S-specific QTLs and 20 D-specific QTLs) were treatment-dependent QTLs. For example, qShl-3B (3B: 190.17 Mb–92.17 Mb) was only detected under D and qMrl-1D (1D: 463.13 Mb–479.13 Mb) was only detected under S. However, qShl-1D (1D: 463.13 Mb–465.13 Mb) and qRn-2A.3 (2A: 703.93 Mb–726.93 Mb) were detected under both S and D, which indicated that these QTLs were sensitive to both S and D and could form part of a response strategy to alleviate stress induced effects.

In addition, a stable QTL, qRn-4B (4B: 27.70 Mb–28.70 Mb) was identified under both CK and D conditions. This confirmed that the expression of this QTL was stable and not affected by D, suggesting that its close linkage marker could be used to select and breed optimal spike characteristics, regardless of drought constraints.

sec.title: Comprehensive evaluation of salt and drought tolerance
sec.p: The used of multiple indicators in a comprehensive PCA can provide a more scientific and rational evaluation of wheat salt and drought tolerance [51]. Furthermore, the use of a PCA in conjunction with the membership function and a cluster analysis has made assessing stress tolerance in crops more reliable and practical. Previous membership function results, grey correlation analysis results, and PCA results have confirmed the accuracy of other regression analyses and have enhanced the scientific reliability of trait identifications [52–55].

Choudhary [56] screened 314 wheat lines (278 linked to cross populations and 36 normal wheat cultivars) under laboratory conditions to evaluate their salt tolerance. A total of 11 highly salt tolerant, 59 salt tolerant, 100 moderately salt tolerant, 137 salt sensitive, and seven highly salt sensitive lines were observed with a distance of 2.2 between each category [56]. Bao et al. [57] used a PCA to transform 24 conventional traits into seven independent, comprehensive indices and 10 drought tolerance indicators were further screened out by a regression analysis. The membership function and cluster analysis results showed that 16 wheat varieties were divided into three categories: drought-resistant, drought-weak sensitive, and drought-sensitive. In this study, a PCA of the salt and drought tolerant coefficients for the eight tested traits extracted six principal components under S and D. Then, the salt tolerance and drought tolerance lines were selected according to their S and D values. However, only tolerant lines, moderately tolerant lines, and sensitive lines were obtained. There was no highly salt tolerant and sensitive variety, which may be due to the close relationships between the lines and the parents being classified as moderately tolerant lines.

sec.title: Potential limitations of this study
sec.p: The method used in this study was the hydroponic experimental method. Compared with field conditions, hydroponics could accurately control the temperature, humidity, and light cycle of wheat. Without the buffering effect of soil, stress symptoms appeared faster and more obvious.

However, there are some limitations of hydroponic conditions, for example, hydroponic solutions cannot simulate the mechanical resistance, microbial communities, or tri-phase (solid/liquid/gas) structure of field soil, leading to discrepancies in root architecture (such as the proportion of fibrous roots and root hair development) compared to field performance. What’s more, certain yield-related traits can not be measured or investigated under hydroponic conditions, which represents the most significant limitation of hydroponic experiments. Hydroponic experiments provide a theoretical foundation for studying wheat’s salt and drought tolerance, however, further research integrating field data is required.

sec.title: Candidate gene analysis of qShl-3B
sec.p: In this study, qShl-3B was identified as a stable major QTL with a total of 56 high confidence genes in the marker interval of this QTL (Table S6). Gene Ontology (GO) analyses revealed that the predicted gene functions of TraesCS3B02G178600 was identical (Table S7): integral component of membrane and transmembrane transport. The homologue of this gene in Arabidopsis thaliana is SLAH3. Drought stress induces stomatal closure and inhibits stomatal opening simultaneously. Zhang et al. [57, 58] found that S-type anion channels SLAH3 mainly inhibit inward K+ channel KAT1 by protein–protein interaction, and consequently prevent stomatal opening in Arabidopsis. These results further strengthen the possibility that TraesCS3B02G178600 are the most likely candidate genes underlying of qShl-3B, and future studies should be conducted to validate these predictions. The predicted gene functions of TraesCS3B02G182200 and TraesCS3B02G182400 were identical (Table S7): membrane, transport and transporter activity. These two genes are associated with aquaporins and may regulate water uptake and intracellular/extracellular ion homeostasis. Hypothesize that they could potentially serve as candidate genes.

In short, this study conducted additive effect and epistatic effect analyses on the KJ-RIL population, identifying a stable major QTL designated as qShl-3B. Within this genomic interval, we designed and developed an Indel molecular marker and performed candidate gene prediction. This study provides useful material for breeding wheat cultivars with salt and drought resistance and lay a theoretical basis for explaining the mechanism underlying salt and drought resistance in wheat.
